about: Tour stops for the interactive Storyraise Analytics demo. Copy uses the product's own labels; every claim is checked against the code cited in `source` (builder repo). American English, no em dashes.

stops.title: Two ways to read your results
stops.tells: The Numbers breaks down who read your report and how they read it. The Story turns the same results into a plain-English summary.
stops.why: Not everyone on your team wants charts. The Story gives leadership and board members the takeaways without any digging.
stops.next: Use The Numbers when you want detail, and switch to The Story when you need something to share.
keepInMind: Everything on this page covers one report. Your Home tab shows reading activity across all of your reports.

stops.title: Highlights, written for you
stops.tells: Storyraise scans your results and calls out what stands out: when readers peak, where visits tend to end, where readers are, and how many constituents come back.
stops.why: It is the fastest way to spot something worth acting on before you dig into the charts.
stops.next: Treat each highlight as a starting question. If most visits end after one section, Section Retention below shows you why.
keepInMind: Highlights only appear once there is enough activity for them to mean something.

stops.title: Constituents Opened and Constituent Returns
stops.tells: How many people on your list opened their personalized link, and how many of them came back for another visit.
stops.why: A return visit is a strong signal. Someone may have come back to finish reading, share the report, or think about giving.
stops.next: Look for returning names in Most Engaged Constituents and reach out while your report is still fresh in their mind.
keepInMind: These counts come from personalized links, so they include only the people you sent a personal link to.
If someone forwards their link, the visit still counts toward the person you sent it to.

stops.title: Views
stops.tells: Every visit to your report, including repeat visits from the same reader.
stops.why: Views show how much reading your outreach created, whether readers arrived from an email, a social post, a QR code, or your website.
stops.next: Compare views with the size of the audience you reached. If activity is lower than you expected, revisit your subject line, timing, or where you shared the link.
keepInMind: Views count visits to the report itself. They are not email opens.
Your own team is left out when Storyraise recognizes a signed-in teammate, and you can exclude staff email addresses or your whole domain.
Reports published before late May 2026 used an older counter, so compare newer reports with other newer reports.

stops.title: Avg. Time Spent
stops.tells: The average total time a reader spent with your report, added up across all of their visits.
stops.why: Compare it with how long your report takes to read. If it takes six minutes and readers average 40 seconds, most are skimming.
stops.next: If readers move quickly, lead with your impact, shorten the opening, and break up long sections.
keepInMind: More time is not always better. A long time on a form can mean confusion rather than interest.
A visit is recorded after the reader leaves, so an interrupted visit may not be fully counted.

stops.title: Where They're Reading
stops.tells: The approximate places readers opened your report from. Select See more for every region and city.
stops.why: Location can reveal interest you did not expect, like alumni who moved away or a board member's wider network.
stops.next: Look for patterns over several weeks, then use clusters to plan regional events or targeted outreach.
keepInMind: Location is approximate. Mobile networks, workplaces, and VPNs can shift city-level results, so focus on broad regions.

stops.title: Most Engaged Constituents
stops.tells: The people who stood out on this report, each with an Engagement Score of zero to three stars.
stops.why: It turns your list into a short, prioritized list for personal follow-up.
stops.next: Start with your three-star readers, and mention what caught their attention so the conversation feels personal.
keepInMind: One star: they spent more time reading than most constituents who opened this report. Two stars: they also viewed at least half of it. Three stars: they also clicked a link or came back.
Stars reflect engagement with this one report, not a person's overall value or relationship with you.
Names appear only for personalized links.

source.note: median benchmark, half the sections, link click or return

stops.title: Intent badges
stops.tells: Badges flag meaningful actions, like clicking a donation link or returning to the report.
stops.why: An action tells you what someone cares about, even if they only read for a few seconds.
stops.next: Match your follow-up to the action. A donation click might call for a giving conversation, while a return visit might call for a friendly check-in.
keepInMind: Badges are separate from stars, so a quick reader who clicks Donate still gets a badge.

stops.title: Where The Clicks Go
stops.tells: Which links readers clicked, grouped by what they wanted to do, from donating to opening a document.
stops.why: Reading shows attention. Clicking shows intent.
stops.next: Use clicks to shape follow-up and to test your calls to action. If few readers click, make your ask easier to find.
keepInMind: The percentage in the middle is out of everyone who opened the report, including readers who never clicked.

stops.title: How They Read
stops.tells: How many sections readers typically view, roughly how long they spend on each, and how many sections your report has.
stops.why: It shows whether readers explore your report or read one part and leave.
stops.next: If readers view only a section or two, make sure your most important story appears early.
keepInMind: Compare sections viewed with sections in the report. Two of eight means most readers never see the back half.

stops.title: Section Retention
stops.tells: The path readers take from section to section. Bigger squares mean more readers, ribbons show where they went next, and the red edge marks where visits ended.
stops.why: It shows where your storytelling holds attention and where readers lose interest.
stops.next: Here, 130 of the 192 readers who started with the Welcome Letter left right after it. Leading with impact could keep more of them reading.
keepInMind: Drag sideways or use the arrow to see later steps.

source.note: section_flow col 0 Welcome Letter v=192 drop=130

stops.title: Top Visit Times
stops.tells: The days and times of day people read your report, starting from when you first published it. Brighter squares mean more visits.
stops.why: Your readers' habits may surprise you. Evenings and weekends are often busy, even though they fall outside typical email advice.
stops.next: Try the date ranges above the chart, then time your next send or reminder for when your readers tend to show up.
keepInMind: Times are shown in your own time zone, so Evening means evening where you are.
Morning is 6 to 11am, Midday 11am to 3pm, Afternoon 3 to 6pm, Evening 6pm to midnight, and Overnight midnight to 6am.

source.note: window starts at first publish; viewer's local time zone

stops.title: Visits Over Time
stops.tells: Visits to your report over the date range you picked for Top Visit Times, by day or, for longer ranges, by week.
stops.why: Spikes usually line up with a send, a reminder, or a post, so you can see which outreach brought readers in.
stops.next: Note when each email or post went out. If a reminder created a spike, plan one for your next report.

stops.title: The Story
stops.tells: A plain-English summary of this report's results: what stood out, people worth a follow-up, and ideas for next time.
stops.why: It is ready to share with leadership, your board, or program staff, with no chart reading required.
stops.next: Download it as a PDF and bring it to your next team meeting.
keepInMind: The Story is written from the numbers on this page. Read it alongside what you already know about your constituents.
